implementation_notes: The mapper is a stdlib call: json.dumps (or pydantic's model_dump_json) turns the graph into text, and SQLAlchemy's JSON/JSONB type binds it to a single column so reads come back as dicts. This is the default because the payload stays language-neutral and safe to read from anywhere; the serializer function can still be wrapped in one repository object to keep the format decision in one place.
code_sketch:
class Diagram(Base):
    __tablename__ = "diagrams"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    graph: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(JSON)      # JSONB / TEXT

session.add(Diagram(id=1, graph={"nodes": nodes}))
session.flush()                                    # one column, one value
loaded = session.get(Diagram, 1).graph             # dict again
pitfalls: The JSON type tracks the attribute itself, so mutating a nested dict in place is not detected; use MutableDict or flag_modified when the graph is edited incrementally.
JSON round trips turn tuples into lists and datetimes into strings unless the column type carries a custom encoder/decoder, so declare the codec on the column instead of at every call site.
A JSON column is only queryable where the database supports it (PostgreSQL JSONB, MySQL JSON, SQLite JSON1); elsewhere the payload is opaque text.

variants.name: pickle payload in a BYTEA/BLOB column
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Python-only realization: pickle.dumps serializes arbitrary object graphs (including cycles) and SQLAlchemy's PickleType stores the bytes in a BLOB while comparing attribute values to detect changes. Prefer it only when the payload stays inside one trusted Python process; the stdlib docs state that unpickling untrusted data can execute arbitrary code, so it is unsuitable for data that crosses a trust boundary.
variants.code_sketch:
class Diagram(Base):
    __tablename__ = "diagrams"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    graph: Mapped[object] = mapped_column(PickleType)   # BYTEA / BLOB
pitfalls: pickle is not secure: unpickling data that could have been tampered with can execute arbitrary code, as the stdlib documentation warns in capitals.
The stream embeds module and class paths, so renaming, moving or refactoring a class makes old values unpicklable (AttributeError/ModuleNotFoundError on load).
PickleType compares values on flush, so a graph without stable equality is rewritten on every flush, and mutated nested state may be written without the application noticing.
